# Mandela Calls on New Generation at Hyde Park Benefit Concert

**LONDON, June 27, 2008** — Nelson Mandela received a thunderous welcome from 46,664 people in London’s Hyde Park on Friday as the former South African president appeared at a star-filled benefit concert hosted by actor and musician Will Smith.

The number of spectators was deliberately symbolic: 46664 was Mandela’s prison number during his 27 years in apartheid jails and later became the name of his global campaign to fight HIV and AIDS.

Mandela, who will turn 90 on July 18, walked slowly onto the stage with his wife, Graça Machel, as the crowd rose in applause and performers gathered behind him. Wearing one of his trademark patterned shirts beneath a dark coat, he smiled and waved before delivering a brief appeal for continued action against poverty and disease.

“Where there is poverty and sickness, including AIDS, where human beings are being oppressed, there is more work to be done,” Mandela told the audience. “Our work is for freedom for all.”

He then directed his message toward younger generations, saying that his advancing age made it necessary for others to continue the causes that had defined his public life.

“It is time for new hands to lift the burdens,” Mandela said. “It is in your hands now.”

The remarks were greeted with prolonged cheering and chants of “Mandela.” Many in the audience raised their arms or held up mobile phones and cameras to capture what was expected to be one of the Nobel Peace Prize laureate’s last major public appearances in Britain.

Smith presided over the event with characteristic energy, mixing jokes and musical introductions with tributes to Mandela’s political legacy. He was joined by his wife, actress Jada Pinkett Smith, as a roster of international performers took the stage during the several-hour concert.

The lineup included Amy Winehouse, Annie Lennox, Leona Lewis, the Sugababes, Razorlight and Queen with Paul Rodgers. South African musicians also featured prominently, underscoring the concert’s connection to Mandela’s homeland and to the 46664 campaign.

Winehouse, whose health and recent public difficulties had generated intense attention, drew one of the loudest responses of the evening. She later joined other artists for the finale, a performance of “Free Nelson Mandela,” the protest anthem written by Jerry Dammers and first recorded by the Special A.K.A. in the 1980s.

Queen guitarist Brian May and drummer Roger Taylor helped bring the show to a dramatic close, with performers crowding the stage as images from Mandela’s life appeared on giant screens. The music alternated between celebration and remembrance, tracing the journey from the international movement demanding Mandela’s release to his emergence as South Africa’s first Black president.

Among the prominent guests were former U.S. President Bill Clinton and other political, cultural and entertainment figures. Recorded and onstage tributes praised Mandela’s role in dismantling apartheid and guiding South Africa through its first democratic elections in 1994.

The concert formed part of a series of events in London marking Mandela’s approaching 90th birthday. But organizers emphasized that the gathering was more than a birthday celebration. Proceeds were intended to support 46664 and its efforts to raise awareness and funding for HIV/AIDS programs, particularly in Africa.

Mandela established the campaign’s identity around the prison number assigned to him after his conviction for sabotage. He was prisoner 466 in the year 1964, producing the number 46664. What had once been a mark imposed by the apartheid state was transformed into a symbol of solidarity and social action.

HIV and AIDS have long carried a deeply personal significance for Mandela. In 2005, he announced that his son Makgatho had died of an AIDS-related illness, an unusually direct disclosure at a time when stigma continued to discourage many African families and leaders from speaking openly about the disease.

Friday’s event also reflected Mandela’s gradual withdrawal from public life. He formally retired from politics after serving one term as president, from 1994 to 1999, and in 2004 announced that he would reduce his public commitments. His appearances had since become less frequent as his health and mobility declined.

Still, his presence briefly transformed the vast central London park into a scene reminiscent of the mass rallies that followed his release from prison in 1990. The audience included longtime anti-apartheid campaigners as well as younger spectators born after Mandela had walked free.

Mandela did not dwell on his own achievements. Instead, he used the occasion to repeat a theme that had become central to his later years: political liberation was incomplete while millions continued to suffer from preventable disease, hunger and inequality.

“After nearly 90 years of life, it is time for new hands to lift the burdens,” he said. “It is in your hands now.”

As he left the stage, supported by Machel, the cheering continued. Behind him, the concert resumed, but its central moment had already arrived: an aging statesman standing before 46,664 people and asking them to carry his work forward.

The event was organized under the banner **46664**—Mandela’s Robben Island prison number—and ticket sales were symbolically limited to 46,664 people. The concert deliberately echoed the **1988 “Nelson Mandela 70th Birthday Tribute” at Wembley Stadium**, held while Mandela was still imprisoned. Broadcast worldwide, that earlier concert helped turn his release and the campaign against apartheid into global popular causes. Twenty years later, Mandela appeared not as a political prisoner but as a former president and international moral leader, making the 2008 gathering both a celebration of his life and a reminder that his work was unfinished.

A central purpose was **HIV/AIDS awareness and fundraising**. The 46664 campaign had evolved into a major vehicle for fighting HIV/AIDS, especially in Africa. The issue was personal for Mandela: his son Makgatho died of an AIDS-related illness in 2005, and Mandela publicly named the cause to challenge stigma and secrecy. Thus, the 2008 concert linked the anti-apartheid solidarity of 1988 with a newer global struggle—encouraging political leaders and ordinary people to act against HIV/AIDS, poverty, and injustice.

# Mandela marks 90th birthday with star-studded London concert

**By CNN-style News Desk**  
**June 27, 2008**

**LONDON** — Nelson Mandela urged a new generation to continue the fight against poverty, disease and injustice Friday as thousands gathered in London’s Hyde Park for a concert celebrating his 90th birthday.

“Where there is poverty and sickness, including AIDS, where human beings are being oppressed, there is more work to be done,” the former South African president told the crowd. “Our work is for freedom for all.”

Mandela, who turns 90 on July 18, received a prolonged ovation after taking the stage alongside his wife, Graça Machel. The concert featured international performers and promoted 46664, Mandela’s campaign to raise awareness of HIV/AIDS.

“After nearly 90 years of life, it is time for new hands to lift the burdens,” Mandela said. “It is in your hands now.”

The campaign’s name comes from Mandela’s prison number: He was the 466th prisoner admitted to South Africa’s Robben Island prison in 1964.

Mandela spent 27 years behind bars for his role in the struggle against South Africa’s apartheid system, including 18 years on Robben Island. His imprisonment made him an international symbol of resistance to racial oppression.

Released in 1990, Mandela helped negotiate the dismantling of apartheid with then-President F.W. de Klerk. The two men shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize.

In 1994, Mandela became South Africa’s first Black president after the country’s first fully democratic election. He served one five-year term, focusing on national reconciliation and efforts to bridge the divisions created by decades of white-minority rule.

After leaving office in 1999, Mandela remained active in humanitarian causes through the Nelson Mandela Foundation and other initiatives. His work included promoting peace, children’s welfare and expanded treatment and prevention programs for HIV/AIDS. He also became a prominent advocate against the stigma surrounding the disease after his son Makgatho died of an AIDS-related illness in 2005.

Friday’s concert brought together political leaders, celebrities and musicians in a tribute that was both a birthday celebration and a call to action.

Mandela closed his remarks with the message that has defined much of his public life: The struggle for justice must continue beyond any one leader or generation.
